title: KV cache — hierarchical segmentation and slabless pool design
content:
Context and intent

This doc proposes a new KV cache architecture that trades away slab rigidity for a hierarchical segmentation + slabless pool allocator. The goal is to reduce long-term fragmentation and improve tail latency by making allocation and eviction decisions aware of workload temperature, NUMA affinity, and entry size distributions. This is an intermediate design (post prototype) intended to replace the current bucketed-slab allocator in the production serving runtime.

High-level goals
- Reduce sustained external/internal fragmentation for real LLM workloads (prefix caching + KV growth over long-lived sessions).
- Keep per-request latency tight (no blocking GC pauses).
- Support multi-tenancy and NUMA-friendly allocation.
- Make eviction cost-aware and stable under shifting token-length distributions.
- Allow incremental rollout and safe rollback; cheap diagnostics and metrics.

Constraints and assumptions
- Typical entry sizes: 128B (small) to several MB (cached large KV for long contexts); heavy-tail distribution.
- Workloads expect low p99 token latency; background work must not affect the p99 if possible.
- Memory budget per node is constrained and needs predictable reclamation.
- We cannot rely on OS-level compaction; we must reduce fragmentation within the runtime.

Design summary (top-level)
1) Hierarchical segmentation: split cache into three logical segments — hot, warm, cold — each with tunable memory budgets. Segments are logical only (no strict separation of address spaces) and influence allocation policies and eviction priorities.

2) Slabless pool allocator: replace rigid slab classes with a hybrid size-class + chunk allocator that:
   - Offers fine-grained small-size classes (power-of-two up to 4KB) for common kv entry headers.
   - Uses a chunked large-allocator for entries >4KB that allocates contiguous run-lengths from per-NUMA arenas.
   - Uses per-thread caches for recently freed small blocks to avoid contention.

3) Compact entry layout: store header + inline short value (<=64B) as single allocation; for large values use 2-part layout (header + external blob) with a compact relocation header to allow moving during background compaction.

4) Eviction policy: a hybrid cost-aware algorithm combining approximate LRU (LRU-2, segmented) with a size-aware cost metric: score = age * weight(size) * underpressure_factor. This penalizes large entries unless they show high reuse.

5) Background compaction and live relocation: a low-priority background worker performs targeted compaction inside warm/cold segments, migrating scattered small free runs into contiguous chunks and relocating live entries to reduce fragmentation. Relocation is done with careful epoching so readers can still access old addresses until swap completes.

Component details
A. Segmentation details
- Hot segment: small dedicated budget (e.g., 5–10% of total kv memory); only contains entries promoted by recent accesses. Eviction is aggressive-LRU. Kept very compact to ensure low-latency hits.
- Warm segment: majority of working set; supports relocation and background compaction. Eviction is cost-aware.
- Cold segment: long-tail items that aren't accessed frequently. We allow coarser-grained memory reclamation (chunk drops).

Promotions/demotions
- On access, entry gets a promotion token; threshold-based promotion to hot. We decay tokens over time (exponential decay) to avoid hot-set drift. Demotion happens when hot budget is exceeded.

B. Allocator
- Per-NUMA arenas: maintain independent arenas to keep allocations local. Each arena provides:
   * size-class freelists up to 4KB, with per-thread caches (TPC) for hot-path alloc/free.
   * large-chunk pool: allocate large contiguous runs (multiples of 4KB pages) from arena-managed huge chunks.
- Slabless characteristic: no fixed pre-allocated slabs for each class; we allocate on demand and reuse freed runs. This avoids long-term wasted slab pages when a model's working set shifts.
- Free list compaction: Freed small blocks are recorded into a local free bitmap and consolidated lazily into free runs for compaction.

C. Entry layout and relocation
- Compact header: 16 bytes (key hash, flags, size class, segment id).
- Inline payload for <=64B.
- For larger payloads: header points to blob location; the blob record contains a relocation pointer used by compaction.
- Relocation protocol: writers allocate new space, copy payload, publish new pointer with a CAS, then retire the old blob into a per-arena tombstone list for reclamation. Readers accept either pointer until epoch advance.

D. Eviction scoring and policy
- Score(entry) = (now - last_accessed) / (1 + reuse_count) * log(1 + size_in_kb) * segment_factor
- When memory pressure rises, we sample candidate sets per arena (stochastic eviction) and pick the highest score candidates to evict. Sampling avoids global locks.

E. Compaction
- Background compactor threads per arena scan warm/cold segments and identify fragmentation hotspots (lots of small freespaces interleaved with live entries).
- For a hotspot, compactor will try to pull live entries into a new contiguous chunk; after successful move, it updates pointers and frees old pages.
- Compaction is rate-limited and coordinated per-NUMA to avoid cross-node memory spikes.

Failure/consistency modes
- If relocation CAS fails, retry with backoff; keep a bounded retry cap to avoid livelock.
- If compactor cannot make progress (high churn), throttle compaction and trigger a fallback coarse eviction (drop entire chunks).

Operational metrics (must instrument)
- fragmentation_ratio = bytes_free_but_unusable / total_allocated_memory
- compaction_throughput (MB/s) and attempts/successes
- per-segment hit rates and p99 latency delta for hits that required relocation
- eviction_samples/sec and average score of evicted entries
- per-arena cross-node allocations and remote access counts

Testing and experiments
1) Microbenchmarks: replay real workload traces (prefix cache + multi-session) on local node to compare fragmentation over 72h with slab allocator vs slabless.
2) Latency impact: measure p50/p95/p99 for small hot hits while compaction running at several intensities.
3) Eviction stability: simulate model switching (sudden shift in typical token lengths) and test memory blowups.
4) NUMA locality: force allocations to remote NUMA to measure remote access penalties and validate arena strategy.

Rollout plan
- Stage 1 (canary): build slabless allocator behind a feature flag. Limit to internal samples and low-traffic clusters. Collect metrics.
- Stage 2 (wider canary): enable for a small percentage of customers, monitor fragmentation, p99 latency, and OOM events for 7 days.
- Stage 3: promote to all production, with capability to revert to old allocator in 30s by draining new arenas and switching pointers.

Open questions and tradeoffs
- Migration: do we support seamless migration of existing slab allocations into the new arena (copying vs retire in-place)? Copy cost may be heavy.
- Header overhead: compact headers increase metadata ops; is the extra CPU worth the memory savings? Run cost/benefit benchmarks.
- Eviction fairness across tenants: should we incorporate tenant-weighted scoring? Proposed later as a policy layer on top.

Action items
- Aisha: implement per-arena freelist prototype (2 weeks).
- Evan: prepare trace-driven fragmentation benchmark harness (1 week).
- Mateo: design relocation CAS helper + epoch API (3 days).
- Priya: add initial metrics to runtime probing (compaction_ratio, per-arena remote allocations) (5 days).

Notes to reviewers
- This is a working draft. Expect code-level details to change but the high-level segmentation + slabless arena approach is what we want to evaluate. Please leave comments inline with targeted concerns (CPU overhead, fallback complexity).

Unresolved TODOs
- Exact size-class breakpoints (experiment with 512B, 1KB, 2KB boundaries).
- Heap/tracing integration for cross-service diagnostics.
